articles.content: A three-year training program will prepare local translators across Southeast Asia to put the Bible into spoken forms—like storytelling and song—for communities that share knowledge by voice, not writing. Three workshops will build translators’ skills from basic to advanced to mentoring, so at least 20 participants gain local expertise. Project Name: Training Oral Translators Across Southeast Asia Implementing Organization: Wycliffe Global Alliance Contact: Evelyn Gan Consultant for Oral Translation Programmes Wycliffe Global Alliance evelyn_gan@wycliffe.net Start date: FY 2026 End date: FY 2028 Summary Across Southeast Asia, many communities pass along their culture through spoken word—storytelling, song, and drama—rather than through reading and writing. For them, hearing the Bible in these natural forms often connects more deeply than a printed text. Oral Bible Translation is expanding rapidly in Southeast Asia, but the region lacks enough trained people to sustain it. Seminary graduates know the Bible but not oral translation. Practitioners already working need a path to advance their skills. And almost no one is ready to step into consultant roles. Without urgent, structured training, this shortage could stall Oral Bible Translation projects across the region. This three-year project will trains local translators and seminary students in oral Bible translation. Participants move through three stages: a foundation workshop, an advanced workshop and consultant-level training, with only those who show strong skills advancing to the next stage. Our goal is for at least 20 participants, with a smaller group becoming fully qualified to guide future translation projects. Half of the trainers will themselves be new, gaining experience so the program can continue and grow after this project ends. By working in collaboration with Wycliffe Thai Foundation, Wycliffe Malaysia, YWAM Chiang Mai, FCBH, Spoken Worldwide and CRU, the project is rooted in strong partnerships that will ensure sustainability and local ownership. articles.title: Bible translation’s future is diverse … and local
articles.summary: The ultimate metric of success is no longer just the distribution of physical books, but measurable transformation of lives through deep, culturally authentic understanding.
articles.summary_zh: 衡量成功的最终标准不再仅仅是实体书籍的分发，而是通过深刻的文化真实理解对生活进行可衡量的转变。
articles.title_zh: 圣经翻译的未来是多元化的……和本地
articles.content: Yaoundé, Cameroon — The landscape of global Bible translation is undergoing a paradigm shift, moving away from traditional, agency-led book printing and toward multimodal translations driven by local communities. At a June 2026 gathering in Yaoundé, translation partners and members of Wycliffe Global Alliance organisations spanning Africa, Europe and Latin America reflected on how Scripture is delivered in the 21st century. Their consensus: The ultimate metric of success is no longer just the distribution of physical books, but measurable transformation of lives through deep, culturally authentic understanding. Community-led translation Dr. Paul Kimbi, the Alliance’s Consultant for Bible Translation Programmes, said Bible translation’s future belongs to community dialogue rather than isolated translation agencies. This emerging approach, known as conversational translation, prioritises localised, grassroots work: listening intimately to communities, engaging them in active storytelling and using locally adapted communication channels. As multiple translation agencies increasingly operate within the same borders, global leaders are urging a shift toward radical collaboration. ‘The multiplicity of agencies is not a hindrance; however, harmony and unity are essential,’ Kimbi said. ‘Unity does not mean uniformity. Each agency, according to its unique strengths, approaches Bible translation as a collaborative piece of God’s global mission.’ Multimodal translations will better serve people from different contexts . Beyond the Book: Multimodal and AI Integration Because cultural contexts vary wildly across the globe, the Alliance’s Africa Area gathering highlighted the urgent need for ‘embodied and multimodal’ translations. This means managing multiple streams of communication simultaneously—integrating oral storytelling, vibrant illustrations, written text and digital media. ‘We do not communicate only with words; we communicate with colours, images, and multimedia,’ Kimbi said. ‘We can no longer consider translation strictly as a written book, but rather as a dynamic multimodal experience.’ This digital evolution naturally intersects with the rise of artificial intelligence. While delegates recognised AI’s immense potential to increase translation speed, optimise efficiency and lower operational costs for minority languages, attendees maintained a stance of strategic caution. ‘Technology accelerates the advancement of Bible translation and language development, but it also creates new strategic responsibilities for leaders and organisations,’ said Etienne Ondoa, a language technology consultant. Staff capacity building, therefore, remains the greatest investment, he said. As technology evolves, the skills required to support it in ministry also evolve. ‘Technological leadership should have a voice in strategic decision-making processes, Ondoa said. ‘Technological decisions increasingly influence ministry outcomes, sound financial resource management, cybersecurity, AI adoption and organisational resilience.’ Etienne Ondoa A Symphony for the Global Church Ultimately, leaders at the event reaffirmed that translation organisations do not operate in a vacuum. They exist to serve the church, which remains God’s primary vehicle for global mission. Kimbi likened the future of the movement to a grand, global arrangement. ‘The particularity of modern Bible translation is that it is a diverse ensemble—an orchestra of varied influences interpreting a magnificent symphony titled ‘Scriptures’ for every language community,’ he said. ‘And in this orchestra, we need everyone: local churches, oral communicators, media creators, literacy specialists and technology partners.’ Story: Lune Prudence Mvondo and Isaac Forchie Photos: Isaac Forchie

articles.title: God’s mission in Africa: ‘There is still much to do’
articles.summary: For both the African and global audiences at the Yaoundé gathering, panel members underscored a fundamental truth: Bible translation is not an isolated academic exercise.
articles.summary_zh: 在雅温得会议上，小组成员向非洲和全球观众强调了一个基本事实：圣经翻译并不是一项孤立的学术活动。
articles.title_zh: 神在非洲的使命： “还有很多事情要做”
articles.content: YAOUNDÉ, CAMEROON — During the Wycliffe Global Alliance Africa Area Gathering, a question was put before delegates: Is the African Church awake? A three-person panel, moderated by Dr. Zac Manyim, Director of the Department of Church and Scripture Engagement at CABTAL (Cameroon Association for Bible Translation and Literacy), delved into the continent’s strategic mission challenges and local breakthroughs. A Call from the Pulpit to Action ‘Yes, the African Church is awake, but it is not active,’ said Rev. Abel Chebe Ngah of the Apostolic Church in Cameroon. He noted a disparity in how modern ministry resources are being spent. ‘Some churches are focused on building megachurches, while only a few are focused on spreading the Word of God. The African church should have been doing exploits, but it is not yet doing so. There are still many areas in Africa not reached by the gospel.’ For the landscape to shift, Ngah argued that mission cannot be treated lightly; the local church must intentionally send missionaries. Demonstrating local ownership, his own denomination dedicates a specific Sunday every year entirely to Bible translation, using it to mobilise believers and raise financial support for CABTAL’s fieldwork. Though some local churches might lack the required financial resources, they offer abundant human and material resources needed in Bible translation. The Lifelong Impact of Mother-Tongue Literacy Pastor Alphonse Gamaldak, president of the Mofu Gudur Inter-Church Committee, said Bible translation reshaped his entire life trajectory. Before receiving any formal education, he learned to read and write in his mother tongue. This linguistic foundation gave him the leeway to master French, eventually leading him to seminary. ‘Yes, the church is awake in Mofu Gudur (a language community of northern Cameroon) because many kids have now grown and seen their lives transformed by the Bible translated into our language,’ he said. The impact extends far beyond the sanctuary. Through mother-tongue functional literacy programmes overseen by the translation project, community members have developed income-generating activities, drastically improving local livelihoods. Today, over 250 literacy teachers are actively instructing inside churches and surrounding villages. Yet, Pastor Gamaldak warned that sustainability requires ongoing investment. ‘There is still much to do,’ he said, ‘like continuing to build the capacity of and support these 250 literacy teachers.’ In 2008, when the Mofu Gudur New Testament was dedicated, the church and the community came together to facilitate the distribution. Five thousand copies were printed, and they were all sold out in the following months. A second run of 4,000 copies was printed. A few years later, it was still hard to obtain a copy. This motivated CABTAL to begin work on the Old Testament, which was dedicated in May 2026. Thanks to the commitment of the local church, the Mofu Gudur people now have a complete Bible. The Takeaway for the Global Alliance For both the African and global audiences at the Yaoundé gathering, panel members underscored a fundamental truth: Bible translation is not an isolated academic exercise. When local churches move from being merely ‘awake’ to being actively engaged, Scripture access unlocks deep spiritual maturity, local resource mobilisation and holistic community development.
